articles.title: Alaska’s decoy scandal brings back the usual suspects for shady election tactics
articles.summary: Marc Elias is back. The notorious Democratic lawyer who played a critical role in the 2016 Russia hoax is again in the news. His law firm has been identified by the New York Times as part of the expanding scandal involving Democratic effort to confuse voters in Alaska with a decoy candidate named Daniel J.…
articles.body:
Marc Elias is back. The notorious Democratic lawyer who played a critical role in the 2016 Russia hoax is again in the news. His law firm has been identified by the New York Times as part of the expanding scandal involving Democratic effort to confuse voters in Alaska with a decoy candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan.

For those familiar with Elias’s checkered history, this is a case of rounding up the usual suspects.

The scandal involving Democratic candidate Mary Peltola has quickly snowballed this week. A New York Times blockbuster investigative report quotes former staff who claim she knew of a cynical effort by her own campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to confuse voters by recruiting and fielding a decoy “Dan Sullivan” candidate in the race against incumbent Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan (R-Alaska). State and federal investigations are now unfolding, with dozens of federal subpoenas raining down on Alaska.

The effort to get voters to cast mistaken ballots is grossly unethical and, even in these rage-filled times, a uniquely disgraceful scheme. Peltola and the Democratic Party had long denied any involvement in the other Sullivan’s candidacy. So when the Times produced evidence that she allegedly knew, and that Democratic staffers and lawyers had been deeply involved from the beginning, many of us were surprised — that is, until the name “Marc Elias” emerged. Then it made more sense.

The Elias Law Group was already in the news this election cycle for threatening reporters with defamation lawsuits if they kept asking questions about the health of former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee for Senate in North Carolina. Earlier, Elias caused a stir during an unsuccessful Democratic gerrymandering effort, raising the idea that Democratic leaders could abolish the entire Virginia government after courts blocked their attempted radical redistricting plan.

The fact that figures such as Peltola and Cooper wanted to be associated with any law firm headed by Elias is itself an indictment of their judgment and standards.

Despite his losses in cases such as National Republican Senatorial Committee v. Federal Election Commission , Elias is still a favorite of many on the left thanks to his aggression and partisan fervor. The controversies that make him notorious to many make him popular with others.

Elias was the general counsel to the Clinton presidential campaign when it secretly funded the infamous Steele Dossier and pushed the false Alfa Bank conspiracy theory . (His fellow Perkins Coie partner, Michael Sussmann, was later indicted but acquitted for making a false statement to the FBI.)

Clinton campaign officials lied to reporters during the 2016 campaign, denying any involvement in the Steele Dossier. Journalists discovered the truth after the election — that the Clinton campaign had hidden payments for the dossier as “legal fees” among the $5.6 million paid to Perkins Coie. New York Times reporter Ken Vogel said that when tried to report the story, Elias “ pushed back vigorously, saying ‘You (or your sources) are wrong .’”

Times reporter Maggie Haberman later observed that “ Folks involved in funding this lied about it, and with sanctimony, for a year .” The Federal Election Commission ultimately sanctioned the Clinton campaign for the subterfuge.

While raising money as the self-proclaimed defenders of democracy, Elias’s group has been involved in gerrymandering and efforts criticized as seeking to invalidate Republican votes, including unsuccessful efforts to challenge Democratic electoral losses.

In Maryland, Elias’s team supported another abusive gerrymandering scheme that a court found not only violated Maryland law but the state constitution’s equal protection, free speech and free elections clauses. The court found that the proposed map “subverts the will of those governed.”

One media site accused Elias and his group of “making millions off gerrymandering efforts” while publicly denouncing Republican gerrymandering.

In 2024, Elias’s legal team was also accused of pushing “to bar third-party presidential candidates — including Cornel West — from swing state ballots where they might siphon votes” from Democratic nominee Kamala Harris.

Likewise, the New York Times reported that the Elias firm’s work “on behalf of a Soros-funded PAC in Texas … was opposed by a left-leaning election watchdog as undermining laws intended to limit the influence of major donors.”

His group’s work for New York’s redistricting effort was ridiculed as not only ignoring the express will of the voters and also effectively negating Republicans’ votes.

In 2024, the Chief Judge of the Western District of Wisconsin criticized the Elias Law Group for one of its challenges. Judge James Peterson (an Obama appointee) said that the argument “ simply does not make any sense .”

Now, Elias’s group is linked to the decoy scandal in Alaska, which allegedly aimed to make voters cast mistaken ballots. What distinguishes lawyers involved in this type of voter disruption is less their talent as their willingness. There are simply some things that most lawyers will not do.

There is also a difference in how lawyers are treated in such controversies. It often seems that in election controversies involving Republican lawyers are more likely to end with bar charges and disbarments. Take John Eastman, the former Trump lawyer disbarred in California after a state bar panel found that he had pushed unfounded legal theories and conspired to obstruct the electoral vote count on Jan. 6, 2021.

Although I publicly disagreed with Eastman’s theories, I opposed the effort to disbar him as setting a dangerous precedent for lawyers seeking to advance novel or unpopular theories of recovery or liability. After all, lawyers on the left routinely advance dubious theories, including some that are more ideologically than legally driven. Such controversies rarely rise to the level of disbarment, especially when more appropriate sanctions are available, ranging from reprimands to fines.

Eastman is currently asking the Supreme Court to overturn his disbarment. It is unlikely that Elias Law Group or Peltola’s lawyers will face similar disbarment efforts — nor should they, in my view, unless they were involved in criminal conduct. But the disparate treatment afforded to counsel in this country by party remains a growing concern. What draws a shower of bar complaints for Republican lawyers brings a windfall of clients for Democratic lawyers.

The New York Times has produced sources alleging that lawyers for Peltola’s campaign were involved in this effort, even though they previously told a federal court that they “lack knowledge or information” and “deny any allegation about those purposes.” Such filings and statements could raise ethical or even criminal questions in investigations at both the state and federal levels.

Meanwhile, though, tens of thousands of voters in Alaska have already cast ballots that included the decoy Sullivan candidate. This could result in a nasty fight in Congress if Peltola prevails in the vote count. And when it happens, that is where we will find Marc Elias in his element.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “ Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution .”

articles.title: Ricketts leads independent candidate Osborn by 6 points in latest Nebraska Senate poll
articles.summary: Just ahead of Election Day, Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) leads his independent challenger Dan Osborn, a new survey of the Nebraska Senate race shows. The New York Times/Siena University poll shows Ricketts leading Osborn by 6 points, 49 percent to 43 percent, respectively, among likely Nebraska voters. November’s election is the second cycle in a…
articles.body:
Just ahead of Election Day, Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) leads his independent challenger Dan Osborn, a new survey of the Nebraska Senate race shows.

The New York Times/Siena University poll shows Ricketts leading Osborn by 6 points, 49 percent to 43 percent, respectively, among likely Nebraska voters.

November’s election is the second cycle in a row in which no Democrat was on the Nebraska Senate ballot. In 2024 and 2026, Democrats backed Osborn instead of supporting their own candidate, hoping to have a better shot at defeating the GOP.

While Osborn has not said he would caucus with one party or the other in the U.S. Senate, most Nebraska voters see him as more aligned with Democrats, the Times poll shows. Fifty-five percent think Osborn is more similar to Democrats, while just 33 percent believe he is more of an independent. Only 4 percent said he was more of a Republican.

Being branded as a Democrat does not get you far in Nebraska, where 71 percent of voters said they were dissatisfied with the Democratic Party.

Still, Osborn is running just 6 points behind in a state President Trump carried by more than 20 points in 2024. The president’s approval is underwater in the Times poll, but just barely — 47 percent approve and 49 percent disapprove of his job performance.

Osborn came within just over 6 points from winning in 2024 as well, when he ran a surprisingly competitive race against Sen. Deb Fischer (R).

Since that campaign however, Republicans have had more time to define Osborn and paint him as a Democrat, which may have hurt his image with voters.

Democrats in South Dakota and Idaho also have no candidate on the ballot and are backing independent challengers to GOP Sens. Mike Rounds and Jim Risch, respectively. Montana Democrats attempted to do the same, backing independent Seth Bodnar against Republican Kurt Alme, but Democrat Alani Bankhead, who won her party’s primary, refused to drop out of the race.

While Ricketts leads in the Senate race, Democrats in Nebraska’s House races are running surprisingly strong. The party is heavily favored to flip the open 2nd Congressional District, and is even contesting the 1st district, represented by Rep. Mike Flood (R), which Trump won by double digits in 2024.

Trump traveled to Nebraska to rally for Ricketts in early October, one of his many stops in deep-red states that his party is struggling to hold in the midterms.

The Times/Siena poll was conducted from Oct. 23 to 29 among 809 likely Nebraska voters. The poll has a margin of error of +/- 4.2 points.

articles.title: Federal appeals court lifts Idaho ruling permitting abortions for women’s health
articles.summary: A federal appeals court paused a judge’s earlier ruling that ordered Idaho to allow exceptions to its abortion ban in cases where a doctor deemed it necessary to protect the mother’s health. In a 2-1 decision issued on Friday, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that a doctor who sued over the state’s…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court paused a judge’s earlier ruling that ordered Idaho to allow exceptions to its abortion ban in cases where a doctor deemed it necessary to protect the mother’s health.

In a 2-1 decision issued on Friday, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that a doctor who sued over the state’s ban was unlikely to prevail on claims that the right to a health-saving abortion is constitutional.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in its 2022 Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision there was no constitutional right to abortion, overturning its landmark 1973 Roe v. Wade decision.

Idaho and a dozen other states issued near-total abortion bans following the high court’s ruling. Abortion is restricted in an additional nine states, according to the Center for Reproductive Rights .

The appeals court’s pause applies to an 81-page decision issued by U.S. District Judge Lynn Winmill in August, which the federal judge later limited to bar the state law’s enforcement against the plaintiff, Stacey Seyb.

“We think it unlikely that Dr. Seyb will be able to square the district court’s perspective on the history and tradition concerning abortions with the Supreme Court’s perspective in Dobbs,” the appeals court said in its decision.

Circuit Judges Kim Wardlaw and Consuelo Callahan made up the court’s majority in this ruling. Wardlaw, a Clinton appointee, issued a concurring opinion, in which she noted that the appeals court was “bound by the decisions of the Supreme Court.”

“As such, in light of the Dobbs majority opinion, I join Judge Callahan in concluding that Defendants have shown a likelihood of success on the merits,” Wardlaw continued.

In a dissenting opinion, Circuit Judge Marsha Berzon found the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision applied only to elective abortions and warned that some women could be “required to continue their pregnancies at serious, permanent risk to their health” because of this ruling.

“The risk, absent the injunction, to Dr. Seyb’s pregnant patients of serious and lasting harm short of death is definitionally a risk of irreparable injury,” she wrote.

articles.title: DC, Virginia sue to block Trump’s triumphal arch
articles.summary: Washington, D.C., and Virginia sued the National Parks Service and Interior Department to block President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch on Saturday, a new court filing shows. The planned arch would resemble arches in other cities, including Paris’s Arc de Triomphe, and be constructed on the border between D.C. and Virginia. In the court filing, the…
articles.body:
Washington, D.C., and Virginia sued the National Parks Service and Interior Department to block President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch on Saturday, a new court filing shows.

The planned arch would resemble arches in other cities, including Paris’s Arc de Triomphe, and be constructed on the border between D.C. and Virginia.

In the court filing, the plaintiffs call the arch “flagrantly unlawful” because Trump did not seek congressional authorization to construct the project.

“In their rush to break ground on the Arch, Defendants have made only half-hearted gestures at complying with these requirements,” the lawsuit reads. “Perhaps recognizing that the project is legally indefensible, Defendants have made clear that they will attempt to outrun judicial review.”

The president has pushed forward with his efforts to renovate Washington despite frequent lawsuits and a lack of congressional authorization. One particular case involved the White House ballroom, in which the East Wing was demolished and construction on the ballroom began immediately.

When sued over the project, the Supreme Court ruled in the Trump administration’s favor after Trump argued the ballroom construction needed to continue for national security purposes.

The plaintiffs in Saturday’s lawsuit say they hope to avoid a similar situation with the arch.

“It is entirely foreseeable that, once construction begins, Defendants will argue—as they have done in other cases—that an order halting construction would irreparably harm the federal government, pose security risks, and impermissibly alter the status quo they have unilaterally created,” the lawsuit reads.

In a statement to The Hill, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones called the project “an affront” to Arlington National Cemetery, where the arch would be located.

“President Trump’s illegal vanity project is an affront to this hallowed ground and the extraordinary sacrifices it represents,” Jones said. “The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place.”

D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb said the lawsuit was filed to prevent “irreparable harm” to the District.

“Construction of the Arch is flagrantly illegal and will cause serious, immediate, and irreparable harm to the District and its residents,” Schwalb said in a statement to The Hill. “We’re filing this lawsuit now to protect DC’s unique interests and critical role in preserving the safeguards that keep our nation’s capital beautiful and safe.”

The Parks Service did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The proposals for the arch at one point included military plans , as Trump said it would be used for snipers and drones, though the final plans submitted to the city did not include the military complex.

Arlington County, Va. previously sued the Trump administration to block the arch in early October.

articles.title: Daylight saving time 2026: Clocks ‘fall back’ an hour tonight. Why is it still so controversial?
articles.summary: Americans will gain an extra hour of sleep on Sunday.
articles.body:
Daylight saving time ends tonight as scheduled, bringing sunsets before 5 p.m. to some cities. At 2 a.m. Sunday, clocks in 48 states will fall back one hour, giving back the hour taken in springtime .

The change will give many an extra hour in bed and brighter mornings, but also earlier sunsets that will last through the winter.

It comes amid an ongoing political tussle to make daylight saving time permanent .

The House easily passed a bill in July to make daylight saving time permanent. It has since moved to the Senate, where it is meeting significant opposition — despite being backed by President Trump. The Senate is unlikely to act before the end of the year, according to the Associated Press .

What dates do the clocks go back, and when do they move forward again?

Under federal law, daylight saving time runs from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November. This year, it began on March 8 and ends at 2 a.m. local time Sunday, Nov. 1, when clocks go back one hour.

Under the current schedule, clocks will spring forward again on Sunday, March 14, 2027.

The clocks going back means earlier darkness for everyone, but it will be more keenly felt in some regions than others.

On Sunday, the sun will set before 5 p.m. in New York City, Chicago, Denver and Seattle, according to AccuWeather , while Caribou, Maine, will see sunset as early as 4:16 p.m., among the earliest in the contiguous U.S.

Later sunsets will be in store in the South, with the sun setting in Houston and Miami at 5:34 p.m. and 5:39 p.m., respectively.

Over the course of November, Seattle will lose more than 70 minutes of daylight, compared with about 30 minutes in cities in the South such as Austin and Tampa, AccuWeather said.

What's happening to the plans to scrap daylight saving time?

In July, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act by 308-117, which would see the U.S. remain on daylight saving time all year.

Several bills to end the twice-yearly clock changes have been introduced in recent years, but the Sunshine Protection Act gained momentum with broad bipartisan support in the House and backing from Trump.

However, the bill faces opposition from senators, including Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, who warned in a 2025 Senate floor speech that permanent daylight saving time "would push winter sunrises to an absurdly late hour, depriving Americans of morning sunshine that's essential for our safety and well-being."

The president has stepped up pressure on Senate Republicans to pass the legislation, even as it remains stalled. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told Politico this month there is "no clear path forward."

"The United States Senate is letting the Daylight Saving Bill die," Trump said in a Truth Social post on Oct. 26, urging the Senate to "TAKE A VOTE!" In a previous Truth Social post, Trump railed against Cotton, saying, "Who wouldn't want more "SUN" in the afternoon than in the morning?"

According to YouGov polling from March 2026, about two-thirds (64%) of Americans say they would like it if clocks no longer changed twice a year, with just 16% preferring to keep the current approach. It also showed more people would prefer the later sunrise and sunset times of daylight saving (43%) than standard time (28%).

Opponents also point to northern states, where winter sunrises would come much later. "You'd be sending kids to school in the dark," South Dakota Republican Sen. Mike Rounds said, according to the AP .

Daylight saving time was adopted in Germany in 1916 to conserve fuel and energy during World War I.

The U.S. adopted it in 1918 under the Standard Time Act, which also created the country's time zones. The change proved unpopular, and Congress repealed it in 1919 over President Woodrow Wilson's veto. Cities and states were left to choose their own schedules.

Congress brought it back in 1942 as year-round "War Time" during World War II, and it ended in 1945. A patchwork of local clock rules followed, until the Uniform Time Act of 1966 set one national schedule and let states opt out, as Arizona and Hawaii have.

The current schedule, running from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November, dates from the Energy Policy Act of 2005, which took effect in 2007.

Who participates in daylight saving time in the U.S.?

Most states observe daylight saving time, but Hawaii and most of Arizona do not. With summer temperatures among the hottest in the country, Arizona has little appetite for daylight saving time, which would extend sunlight into the evening during the hottest part of the year.

Hawaii's sunrises and sunsets follow a fairly set schedule because of its close proximity to the equator. By sticking to one time all year round, Hawaii Standard Time, islanders can follow the flow of the sun, according to KHON-TV .

The Navajo Nation, however, which spans three states, including Arizona, observes daylight saving time.

images.caption: This instalation by artist Donald Lipski, 'Time Piece', at the El Monte Transit Station will "fall back" one hour for the time change on November 1. (Myung J. Chun via Getty Images)
This AccuWeather graphic shows what areas of the U.S. will lose the most daylight over November.

articles.title: How Obama appointee and Trump nemesis Boasberg ended up overseeing Ilhan Omar warrant, other key cases
articles.summary: Judge James Boasberg oversees the Ilhan Omar search warrant fight, deportation flights, and California voter rolls, raising assignment questions.
articles.body: Federal Judge James Boasberg, dubbed a "Radical left lunatic" by President Donald Trump, is presiding over several high-profile cases challenging actions made by the Trump administration, raising questions about how judges are assigned to cases. The scrutiny comes as Boasberg, an Obama-appointed chief judge of the Washington, D.C. district court, oversees a challenge brought by several media outlets seeking to force the Justice Department to unseal the search warrant on the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., stemming from two federal investigations. "Judge James Boasberg is now involved with the Ilhan Omar case," Steve Ferguson, a self-described business owner with more than 250,000 followers on X, wrote in a social media post. "Is everything rigged?" In the federal court of the District of Columbia, cases are assigned to judges randomly by an electronic system managed by the clerk's office operating under the direction of the Calendar and Case Management Committee, according to the rules of the court. The committee consists of three to five judges appointed by the chief justice. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION There are exceptions to the random-assignment process. For example, criminal grand jury matters are assigned to and overseen by the chief judge, currently Boasberg. This means Boasberg’s assignment to oversee the fight over unsealing the search warrant for Omar was "not a surprise" to Eric Wessan, Iowa’s solicitor general. "But there are a lot of cases that seem to be going to judges maybe based on those cases having similarities which is not what the local rules say," Wessan told Fox News Digital. When a case needs to be reassigned, the Calendar and Case Management Committee will determine how the reassignment is made. Wessan suggested that concerns over how case assignments are made is valid, considering some of the high-profile cases against the Trump administration which have appeared in Boasberg's docket. "If one is just following anecdotally, there does seem to be a lot of high-profile cases in front of judges that seem to be expressing unusual amounts of frustration or disagreement with the administration," Wessan said, urging greater transparency in how case assignments are made. TRUMP’S FIGHT OVER RARELY USED 18TH-CENTURY DEPORTATION LAW LIVES ON IN LATEST COURT CLASH The fight over unsealing the release of Omar's search warrant is just one of several cases involving the Trump administration and now on Boasberg's docket. Boasberg is also overseeing California’s lawsuit against the Trump administration over voter-roll disputes. On Friday, he ordered the administration to provide the state with the names and supporting information for roughly 20,000 people whom the DOJ claims are noncitizens on California’s voter rolls by the end of the day. Boasberg has issued several consequential rulings against the Trump administration, including a high-profile March 2025 order directing the administration to turn around deportation flights carrying alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador. The Trump administration fought against the order, pointing to the Alien Enemies Act as legal justification for the deportations. The dispute over the administration’s use of the Alien Enemies Act eventually reached the Supreme Court, which vacated Boasberg's temporary restraining order blocking deportation flights, ruling that the case was brought in the wrong jurisdiction. That same month, Boasberg was assigned a lawsuit seeking to preserve Signal messages after top Trump administration officials discussed plans for a Yemen strike in a group chat that accidentally included Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg. He later ordered the administration to preserve the messages. The string of cases prompted Reps. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, Darrell Issa, R-Calif., and Chip Roy, R-Texas, to send a letter in May 2025 to the court clerk asking for greater clarity on how judicial assignments are made. The lawmakers questioned whether assignments were truly random, as the court’s rules state. "The Committee cannot independently verify the randomness of case assignments because the composition of assignment decks is kept secrets," the lawmakers wrote. "We must understand the nature of the case assignment process in the District Court—which is considering a number of cases challenging the Trump Administration’s policy decisions—to consider and develop appropriate legislation," the lawmakers wrote. FEDERAL JUDGE KICKED OFF 'BOTCH JOB' ANTI-DEI CASE AFTER STUNNING APPEALS COURT REBUKE Meanwhile, Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced legislation in July that would require federal district courts to assign cases randomly, without exceptions, naming it the Boasberg Act. The bill is currently stalled in committee. "Judge Boasberg is the poster child for a rogue judge and exposed serious loopholes in our judicial system. Randomly assigning cases among judges ensures the American people can have confidence in the impartiality of our courts," Schmitt said in a statement. Under the rules of D.C. Court, the chief justice does not have the power to reassign a case. The Calendar and Case Management Committee handles case reassignments. The court must notify the judges and attorneys involved, but it does not have to publicly explain why a case was reassigned. Wessan has called for greater transparency. "The rules shouldn’t say one thing if it’s not true. But if it is true, they could just say so. I think the issue is with the exceptions—what happens in those exceptional cases and how often do they occur?" Wessan said. articles.title: Christian group touts 'ethical' tech features as concerns over out-of-control AI tools persist
articles.summary: Ligonier Ministries built its "Grow" app with an AI assistant that deflects vulnerable users to real humans and the suicide hotline when needed.
articles.body: The leader of a Christian ministry that built its own artificial intelligence application to guide users in their spiritual journey warns companies developing AI systems need to implement "ethical guidelines" to ensure their technology doesn't harm people. Ligonier Ministries president and CEO Chris Larson says that the true highest intelligence is God, and shared a new tool his group created to help answer questions people my have from a faith-based perspective. "It's interesting that [President Donald Trump] even referred to artificial intelligence now as 'superintelligence,'" Larson told Fox News Digital. "Of course, Christians — and, really, all of us — have access to the 'superintelligece,' the one who has created the universe." CHRISTIAN UNIVERSITY AIMS TO PRODUCE 'IRREPLACEABLE' GRADUATES AS AI RESHAPES HIGHER EDUCATION The mission of the Florida-based organization, founded by the late Christian theologian R.C. Sproul, is to proclaim, teach and defend the holiness of God "in all its fullness to as many people as possible." Part of accomplishing that mission was building an app that the organization calls "Grow." "It's dedicated to helping Christians to better understand the Bible and theology and to go deeper in their faith, put down roots, if you will," Larson said of the new tool. "And so this app has 50 years of teaching in it from more than 800 different teachers, of course, grounded in Dr. R.C. Sproul's lifetime of teaching." The app draws from a library of tens of thousands of pieces of content help users in their faith journey looking to obtain answers to critical questions. Inside Grow is an "intelligent answer assistant" which can answer questions from users from a faith-based perspective. But building an Grow for Christian users required putting a great deal of thought into the ethics of the model, Larson explained. WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL "Now, it's not trying to pretend it's a person or anything like that. It is just trained on our library, and then helping Christians to trust the answers, and [it] will only go so far," he said. "And again, I think that's an important guard as well. Because for us, making sure that we have trusted theological answers and that the intelligent answer assistant is acting with integrity and not going outside of that." When a user pushes the boundaries of the application, it directs them to real human support — a feature most large language model AI tools refuse to implement. "And so we've given it a sandbox to work within, and any time that somebody tries to push it beyond the borders, we're going to deflect or defer to a real human. Imagine that," Larson said. For example, if a user discusses suicidality in Grow, the intelligent answer assistant will direct them to the suicide hotline or other real-world resources. BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: POPE LEO SEES THE AI AGE CLEARLY — AND WARNS WE MUST SAVE OUR SOULS Over the past several years, there have been a flurry of suicide deaths that victims' family members say AI chatbots were at least partially responsible. In one case from last year, a teenager named Adam Raine took his own life after months of discussing his suicidal thoughts on ChatGPT. According to a lawsuit from his parents, the chatbot provided him information about methods of suicide, validated aspects of planning the suicide and offered to help him draft a suicide note. OpenAI, ChatGPT's parent company, disputes the characterization and says the chatbot directed him to crisis resources multiple times. "So, we understood that it's important to provide safety guardrails, but also we did not want this intelligent answer assistant to pretend that it was a person," said Larson. "We don't want it to take the place of a pastor or a local church elder or even a parent." WHO IS DARIO AMODEI, THE ANTHROPIC CEO PUSHING INDEPENDENT AI OVERSIGHT? Larson said companies developing AI need to consider guardrails for their technology. "Anybody developing AI tools today needs to think through ethical guidelines, and that's more of the self-regulation and guardrails that we've been talking about," he said. "I think there's a real concern today because you have great power that's been entrusted to these different companies and they're not really disclosing their worldview," he continued. "How do they know right from wrong?" For Ligonier, the absolute truth upon which its AI model is built is the Christian faith. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

articles.title: The 6 races that could decide Senate control
articles.summary: The midterm tug-of-war for Senate control will come down to half a dozen coin-toss contests, giving both parties a path to the upper chamber majority. All six seats rated as “toss-ups” by DDHQ — Texas, Maine, Alaska, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas — are currently held by Republicans. The GOP’s best chance of flipping a seat…
articles.body:
The midterm tug-of-war for Senate control will come down to half a dozen coin-toss contests, giving both parties a path to the upper chamber majority.

All six seats rated as “toss-ups” by DDHQ — Texas, Maine, Alaska, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas — are currently held by Republicans. The GOP’s best chance of flipping a seat is in Michigan, where DDHQ gives Democrats a 73 percent chance of winning.

As of the Friday before Election Day, DDHQ’s forecasts showed Democrats with the advantage in both chambers — though their chances were more uncertain in the Senate, with a 60 percent chance of a flip, than in the House, where they had an 82 percent chance.

Here’s what to know about the races that will decide Senate control:

The Senate race in Texas has been one of this cycle’s most closely watched, from Democrat James Talarico’s rising-star bid amid GOP-friendly redistricting to incumbent Sen. John Cornyn’s (R) dramatic loss to Attorney General Ken Paxton in a tough Republican primary runoff.

It’s become one of the most expensive non-presidential contests in U.S. history, pulling in more than half a billion dollars in what both sides frame as an existential fight for the Lone Star State’s political future.

Texas Democrats haven’t won a statewide race in decades, but they’re hopeful that Talarico’s unity-focused, faith-driven bid can compete with Paxton’s controversy-laden, MAGA-faithful campaign amid frustration with the White House.

Mere days before the election, Talarico was leading Paxton by just under four points in polling averages from DDHQ, with a 60 percent probability of flipping the seat. A recent Emerson College Poll found the race in a dead heat and noted that Libertarian candidate Ted Brown could pull some support on Election Day, potentially tipping the race in Talarico’s favor.

Hispanic and Latino voters could also be a game-changer. The bloc, which makes up roughly a third of the Texas electorate, moved toward President Trump in 2024, but appears to be returning to the left this cycle, frustrated by the president’s handling of the economy and immigration.

One of Democrats’ toughest flip opportunities will be in Iowa, where Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson hopes to hold back Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek in the race to replace retiring Sen. Joni Ernst (R).

According to DDHQ’s Friday forecasts, Hinson was headed into Election Day with a 55 percent chance of holding onto her seat as she led Turek by a single point in polling averages.

“Both Democrats and Republicans privately believe that if only one GOP candidate in our Toss Up states hangs on, it will be Iowa,” Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor wrote in an analysis ahead of the election, noting that Hinson has “deftly distanced herself” from some of Trump’s unpopular policies.

But Trump is still “deeply underwater” in Iowa, Taylor said, and Democrat Rob Sand’s gubernatorial bid could also be key to helping turnout for Turek.

“Ultimately, Democrats are poised to capitalize on Trump’s tumbling image and discouraged base. The true test may be whether even the best GOP candidates of the cycle — in Maine and Iowa — can survive a looming blue wave.”

Former Sen. Sherrod Brown’s (D) comeback bid in Ohio could restore Democrats to the Buckeye State’s Senate delegation just two years after he lost to Sen. Bernie Moreno (R).

Brown is challenging incumbent Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vice President Vance’s Senate vacancy, in the special election to fill out the rest of Vance’s term, which runs through 2028.

Alongside Texas, it’s become one of the priciest-ever Senate races. Brown brought in $23.1 million to Husted’s $5 million in the third quarter alone, but GOP-aligned groups have surged more than $100 million into the state to attack Brown.

Husted has Trump’s support — including comments on his physique that have gone viral in the closing days of the race — but Brown boasts higher name recognition and rare success as a Democrat in the red-leaning state.

As of Friday afternoon, Brown had a 55 percent probability of flipping the seat as he led Husted by roughly 3 points in DDHQ’s polling averages, according to The Hill’s partner.

“After Texas, Ohio is the next most vulnerable GOP-held seat on our list,” Taylor wrote for Cook Political Report, pointing out that Husted has probably been hurt by Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s troubled campaign for Ohio governor.

Sen. Susan Collins (R) is aiming for a sixth term as a rare Republican to win in blue-leaning Maine. She’s been bolstered by her political legacy and name-ID as Democrats dealt with a tumultuous primary season.

But her challenger, Democrat Troy Jackson, is still favored to beat her. The former state Senate president, who unsuccessfully ran for governor this cycle, replaced progressive oyster farmer Graham Platner on the ticket when Platner’s bid imploded amid sexual misconduct allegations.

In a state that went to Vice President Harris in the 2024 presidential election, Collins is leaning on her seniority and stressing her distance from Trump — particularly on tariffs, which have strained Mainers’ pocketbooks and caused problems with Canada, a vital trading partner that shares a 600-mile border with the Pine Tree State.

But though she’s long enjoyed comfortable reelection numbers, she won by a narrower 9 points in 2020 after her controversial vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, which has continued to dog her in 2026.

Jackson had climbed to a 60 percent chance of ousting Collins in DDHQ’s Friday forecast, leading the incumbent by roughly 3 points in polling averages.

Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century, so its “toss-up” rating tees up what could be one of the cycle’s biggest surprises.

Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor and former Republican, has put Sen. Roger Marshall (R), an OB-GYN backed by Trump, on defense in the red stronghold.

In DDHQ’s Friday forecast, Marshall had dropped to a 53 percent chance of holding the seat for the GOP, as Hamilton climbed to a polling-average lead of nearly three points.

As of Friday, Democrats had spent $16 million more on the race than Republicans, according to data tracked by AdImpact.

Experts see the latest numbers out of Kansas as a clear sign of Democratic momentum across the country in this year’s midterms.

“A Democrat winning Kansas, even if that candidate is leading the polls, has got to be considered an upset,” said Decision Desk HQ’s chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley.

“If Democrats win Kansas, not only is it winning a state that they haven’t won in a Senate race since 1932, the longest such drought in the country for either major party, but … for the Senate control question, it gives Democrats sort of an additional card to play,” he said. “If they were to win Kansas, maybe they don’t need to flip Iowa. Maybe you know, maybe Alaska, you know, is less of a concern now.”

Alaska offers Democrats another serious pickup opportunity in what should have been a longshot based on recent trends.

Democrat Mary Peltola, who lost Alaska’s at-large House seat in 2024, is running on a “fish, family, freedom” platform as Sullivan touts his Trump alignment in the red state.

Peltola had a 60 percent shot of taking the seat in DDHQ’s Friday forecast, and was ahead by less than two points in the polling average.

But neither candidate was polling past 50 percent, opening up the possibility that the race kicks into a second round of ranked-choice tabulations. Maine is the only other state with ranked-choice voting statewide. Alaska’s sprawling map with isolated communities lets ballots be counted up to 15 days after the election, provided they were postmarked in time — which could prolong the suspense after polls close on Tuesday.

The race was also rocked in its home stretch by controversy over a candidate with the same name as the incumbent.

The Trump administration filed a lawsuit in late October seeking to block certification of the Senate election if the incumbent loses with Daniel J. Sullivan, who goes by Dan Sullivan, also on the ballot. Peltola’s campaign and national Democrats denied New York Times reporting this week that they coordinated to recruit candidates who could pull support from the sitting senator.

articles.title: Will Tuesday be a a blue wave or just an anti-Trump surge?
articles.summary: All partisan roads seem to lead back to Donald Trump.
articles.body:
Poll after poll shows the Democrats comfortably retaking the House come Nov. 3, with a number also giving them a slightly better than even chance of taking the Senate . Maybe. But I’ve been around this business a long time, and something feels a bit less “bluey” by the day.

To be sure, the Republican brand is in a world of hurt right now, with tens of millions of voters not willing to let the party wiggle off the hook of accountability, since Republicans control the White House, the Senate and the House. Blaming the Biden administration may work with much of the MAGA base, but it frays into incredulity for the rest of the voting blocs when they stop to realize that the Trump administration has been in power for coming up on two years.

Not surprisingly to anyone paying the remotest bit of attention over the last decade, in one way or another, all partisan roads seem to lead back to President Trump. Somewhat ironically for this election cycle, should the Republicans lose across the board, it was Trump himself who blazed one of those rhetorically poisonous roads back to him and his party by repeatedly telling Americans, “ Vote as if I am on the ballot .”

To be sure, millions of Americans in and out of the MAGA base still strongly believe in the president, his brand and his policies. Many believe he saved our nation. But viewing the flip side of that coin, some could certainly make the case that a large percentage of the votes Joe Biden got in 2020 and Kamala Harris got in 2024 were not votes for those two Democratic presidential nominees so much as votes against Trump. If one buys into that theory, then it’s also reasonable to believe that the “I only voted because I want Trump gone” demographic is still out there — and may have grown in the last few years. Such voters are eager to accept Trump’s challenge.

Many Republicans I speak with believe that their party is bleeding votes, from independents, youths. minorities, even faith-based votes. And the main reason for the vote bleed is absolutely no mystery. The administration can sing the praises of a rising stock market and growing 401(k)s until they are blue in the face. These positives mean little or nothing to voters whose paychecks are shrinking by the month as they cope with higher gasoline and grocery prices, home ownership increasingly out of reach, and a widening disappointment regarding the war with Iran.

The pendulum that determines national elections regularly is pushed to that cycle’s winning side by just slivers of the vote in certain districts, counties and states. At the moment, that pendulum is swinging back to the left, even despite a veritable laundry list of accomplishments authored by this president and his administration over the course of the last two years: historically lower crime rates; a closed and protected border; increased energy dominance; and the creation of almost 70 million Trump Accounts for kids.

Even so, many Trump supporters and Republicans still refuse to believe that a blue wave is about to swamp their president and party. They honestly wonder how they could be losing to nothing but sheer hatred of Donald Trump. While the Democratic leadership understandably pounces on the “affordability” issue at every opportunity, their own answers to that “crisis” are either paper-thin or nonexistent.

And yet, the polls continue to favor them.

Is that enough for the Democrats to have a great day on Nov. 3, even with no real solutions to the issues plaguing this nation? We’ll just have to wait and see.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

articles.title: Why the Ilhan Omar saga isn't going away
articles.summary: Trump claims Ilhan Omar must resign from Congress over alleged immigration fraud, but the Constitution grants that power solely to the House itself.
articles.body: President Donald Trump has his favorite riffs during campaign rallies. He’s recently complimented the physique of Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. He still calls out former President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris. But in recent weeks, the president spun Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., into heavy rotation on his playlist. The Department of Homeland Security and Justice Department are now probing Omar for alleged immigration fraud and financial disclosure reports. TRUMP SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD GO TO JAIL OR BE DEPORTED, CALLS HER ‘A DISGRACE TO OUR COUNTRY’ "What she did was use a fake name and other things that are fake," the president groused about Omar. "She used the fake name to be sworn in. I assume she must immediately resign from Congress." Trump argued that Democrats "just conceded her seat." They didn’t. And the president declared that "she will not be legally allowed to be a member of that august body of politicians." Not accurate. The president doesn’t decide who gets to sit in Congress. Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution grants that power to the House and Senate. It charges both bodies with authority to "be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members." The Constitution goes on to say that the House and Senate may "punish its Members for Disorderly Behavior; and, with the Concurrence of two thirds, expel a Member." We bring up those responsibilities because it’s possible that the House may need to tangle with the "qualifications" of Omar. Especially since the New York Times reported that the Minnesota Democrat faced scrutiny by the Obama-era Justice Department in 2016. Moreover, that inquiry says the feds found evidence that she may have entered into a fraudulent marriage. If that’s the case, there could be questions about Omar’s citizenship. And thus, whether she’s even permitted to serve in Congress. Especially if it’s found she was naturalized as a citizen via bogus means. Republicans have been after Omar for years. Across the aisle, Democrats are concerned this could be a distracting headache. Especially if they seize control of the House after the midterms next week. THE HITCHHIKER'S GUIDE TO WHY REMOVING ILHAN OMAR FROM CONGRESS COULD BE HARDER THAN TRUMP EXPECTS The inquiry into Omar began in 2016 when she ran for the state legislature. Former President Barack Obama was in office. The investigation continued into the Biden administration. The feds terminated the inquiry in 2021. After the Trump administration raided Omar’s home in October — seizing electronics and documents — Obama defended the congresswoman. "It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say," the former president said. "But that’s exactly what the Trump administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar." Obama said the current inquiry flipped her life "upside down" and characterized it as an effort to "intimidate someone." Controversial influencer and livestreamer Hasan Piker asked Omar about how her week was going amid the investigation. "It tracks for me," replied Omar. "That’s kind of what I’m used to." A spokeswoman for Omar said that she "has repeatedly and unequivocally denied this baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory." But indications that Omar faced scrutiny ten years ago make it harder to characterize this as wild, right-wing conjecture emanating from the blogosphere. "Who ordered [the investigation] closed?" asked Fox contributor Paul Mauro. "Reportedly, both administrations had opened cases into this. We now know how much smoke there is." Omar campaigned for the state legislature in 2016. Her campaign released a letter from the U.S. attorney saying it "wasn’t investigating" nor requesting an inquiry into Omar. So was she cleared? Or does word of the old probe pour petrol on the flames? "Omar will talk about and say, ‘They've looked into this. Nothing came about it,’" said University of Minnesota political science professor Kathryn Pearson. "But I think it's also a talking point that Republicans will use. So I think sort of both sides will try to use that to their advantage." John Nagel is Omar’s Republican opponent on the ballot next week. Nagel views the new investigation as a political wedge. "With the raid on her home, people should keep this in mind. It's a very serious accusation," Nagel said. "As far as I'm concerned, Somalia comes first in her life. And we are nothing more than a piggy bank for her." TRUMP PUSH TO OUST OMAR FACES HISTORIC SUPREME COURT TEST, BUT LEGAL EXPERTS SEE ‘UNCHARTED’ TWIST At least one Republican is ready to bounce Omar from the House. "If the evidence shows that she is not an American, she has to be removed immediately and probably put in prison," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "I think the idea that a foreigner might be actually serving in Congress should be terrifying to Americans." But another House Republican urges caution. "We just need all the facts," said Rep. Chris Smith, R-N.J. "I hope that the investigation is thorough, fair, and absolutely aboveboard." And then there is the question of due process. "The Ethics Committee should commence an investigation. It takes two-thirds of the House to expel a sitting Member. I would highly doubt the Democrats would agree. And certainly not without findings," Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., told Fox. "I think at a minimum, the Ethics Committee should move forward with an investigation immediately upon our return." This could develop into a real hornet’s nest for the House when lawmakers descend on Washington after the midterms. That’s to say nothing of questions about seating Omar when the new Congress starts in January. If Democrats win the House, would House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. — perhaps as speaker — be forced to grapple with the question of seating Omar if Republicans move to exclude her? In fact, such a motion to exclude comes right before the new speaker swears in the entire House on Jan. 3. The speaker would swear in 434 members. Then takes votes related to the potential member in question. If Democrats win the House, new, moderate House Democrats might take their first formal floor vote on whether to seat Omar. Voting against Omar might be good for some of these new members, considering the political nature of their battleground districts. But would the Democratic brass pressure new members to vote with the caucus on such a nettlesome issue? Democrats who vote to seat Omar give Republicans an immediate opportunity to build a case against newly-christened members representing swing districts. A vote to exclude or expel Omar would go down as one of the most important roll calls of the entire two-year Congress. We haven’t even explored how progressives and Democratic Socialists — new to the House — might rage at moderate Democrats for not supporting their colleague. That could produce a serious schism among Democrats. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP This isn’t going away. Omar is a lightning rod. The GOP believes it can continue to milk this. President Trump has his favorite riffs about Omar. And it’s possible that House Republicans may as well.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo gives Amy Acton flowers at Columbus concert
articles.summary: Pop star Olivia Rodrigo delivered flowers to Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) during her tour stop in Columbus on Friday night, a show of support in the close contest. While performing her song “stupid song,” Rodrigo walked through the crowd at the Schottenstein Center on The Ohio State University’s campus, handed flowers to Acton…
articles.body:
Pop star Olivia Rodrigo delivered flowers to Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) during her tour stop in Columbus on Friday night, a show of support in the close contest.

While performing her song “stupid song,” Rodrigo walked through the crowd at the Schottenstein Center on The Ohio State University’s campus, handed flowers to Acton and embraced her.

During her first show in Columbus, Rodrigo wore an “Amy Acton for Governor” shirt, showing her support for the Democratic nominee who is locked in a competitive race against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy.

“Ohio loves you,” Acton wrote on the social platform X, with an image of Rodrigo wearing the campaign shirt.

Ramaswamy drew controversy for running an ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, who calls her daughter a “liar” and says she is unfit for office.

Acton’s stepfather was charged with sexually abusing Acton at a young age, and Acton was removed from her mother’s custody at age 12. Acton’s mother stayed with their stepfather until his death, the campaign said.

The ad prompted blowback from both parties, including Ohio’s current Republican governor, Mike DeWine, who said the ad should be taken down. Ramaswamy’s campaign put millions behind airing the ad statewide, but it recently came down after running its cycle on the air.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Acton a 61 percent chance of beating Ramaswamy.

Rodrigo has supported political causes in the past, namely reproductive rights. After a leaked draft opinion of the Supreme Court’s ruling in Dobbs v. Jackson, Rodrigo called out the decision at one of her concerts.

“I couldn’t pass up the opportunity to talk about how heartbroken I am over the Supreme Court’s potential decision to overturn Roe v. Wade,” Rodrigo said at the concert.

The singer recently raised $20 million for women’s health at an August benefit concert.

And when the Trump administration posted social media videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids using Rodrigo’s music, she condemned the move and later told NPR that she thinks the administration is baiting pop stars into a response.

articles.title: There’s home in these hills: West Virginia isn’t AI’s dumping ground
articles.summary: As I stare into a forest filled with waving ferns, flitting juncos and towering cherry trees, I worry that AI is destroying the very places where the essence of humanity still exists.
articles.body:
There’s a joke that West Virginia is always 25 years behind. We’re not up on the latest fashion, we drive old cars and some of us still use landlines. The reality is, roughly 80 percent of West Virginia households don’t have reliable, high-speed internet . We also have the lowest artificial intelligence use in the country.

Yet we’re now being dragged at breakneck speed into a digital future that isn’t ours.

AI is hollowing out our way of life in Appalachia. Data centers are leveling our hills and hollers into muddy expanses that flood our homes , pollute our rivers and poison our air . Families are being pushed out of the only places they’ve ever belonged.

As I stare into a forest filled with waving ferns, flitting juncos and towering cherry trees, I worry that AI is destroying the very places where the essence of humanity still exists. I live in Davis, West Virginia, a town of 600 people nestled in the Allegheny Highlands. We grow our food, build our homes, fix our cars and always pass things along before throwing them away.

I can walk for miles in the woods without seeing a soul, but I can’t go to the grocery store without bumping into a friend. We recognize the value not only in our grit, but also in our kindness.

We may live small, but our lives are overflowing with connection, purpose and a steadfast sense of place. In a small town, people know your name. There’s room to carve out a niche and contribute in your own way. Yet, we live among some of the oldest and most biodiverse mountains in the world. The joy of living in Appalachia is feeling our significance while being constantly humbled by the vast array of life around us.

Now that world is being transformed. West Virginia is being sold out to the lowest bidders in the AI race due to a 2025 bill that fast-tracks power plant and data center developments while stripping power from communities . By removing guardrails and preempting local control, our state legislators sent a resounding message to out-of-state interests: West Virginia is for sale. Our people don’t matter.

State officials, speculative developers and out-of-state AI companies tout empty promises of economic benefits and good-paying jobs, while overlooking the costs and brushing off our concerns . A representative from the Virginia-based company that aims to build a 10,000-acre power plant and data center complex in my hometown, said people like me live in “ the middle of nowhere .” The company’s proposed power plant is “ just a drop in the bucket .”

Those building AI and hyperscale data centers are fighting ever faster to create something that aims to replace us. They are obscuring the line between person and computer, while driving a wedge between humanity and the living world. To achieve this, they’ve worked with seeming indifference to transform our farms and forests into rows of lifeless warehouses. Rural communities are bearing the burden of this digital future, but it’s also a future we don’t want.

The future I dream about is already here. It’s in the mountains, gardens, neighborhood bike rides, locally owned businesses and town hall meetings. It’s knowing I can always call a friend for help, and if I’m out of service (which is often), it’s knowing a stranger will stop to ask if I’m ok. It’s in the hearts of West Virginians who fight every day for clean water, healthcare, public school resources, land protections, childcare support and a meaningful local voice.

The beauty of Appalachia is that we don’t just look at our mountains from afar — we are part of them just as they are part of us. In some ways, rural places harken back to an older way of life. But they also offer roadmaps for a more humane future. We know the harm caused by endless extraction. Our future is saying no to yet another extractive industry and saying yes to the way of life West Virginians have already built together.

Beyond threatening our land, water and way of life, AI has called into question what it means to be human and what kind of society we want to live in. It’s been difficult to confront these questions, but it’s also brought the answers into stark relief. Regardless of age, background, location, religion or our politics, the vast majority of us have known the answers all along.

Our future is being human — together — in each little pocket of the planet we call home.

articles.title: Virginia and D.C. sue to stop proposed Trump arch
articles.summary: Virginia and the District of Columbia filed a lawsuit in federal court Saturday in a last-ditch effort to stop the construction of the triumphal arch planned for Memorial Circle in Washington.
articles.body: Virginia and the District of Columbia filed a lawsuit in federal court Saturday in a last-ditch effort to stop the construction of the triumphal arch planned for Memorial Circle in Washington. The Trump administration has said it plans to begin construction of the arch next week, on Nov. 5. “The construction of the Arch will inflict immediate and irreparable harm on the District and Virginia,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb wrote in the lawsuit. “The Arch is slated to be built on a busy traffic circle that abuts the border between the jurisdictions, at the center of a historic viewshed, in a river whose environment the District has a statutory responsibility to protect.” “Both the construction of the Arch and the completed monument will disrupt the operations of both jurisdictions, impair their ability to carry out their responsibilities under federal and local law, and require the expenditure of substantial resources to mitigate and address those impacts,” they added. The attorneys general wrote that their request to block construction is urgent. “It is entirely foreseeable that, once construction begins, Defendants will argue, as they have done in other cases, that an order halting construction would irreparably harm the federal government, pose security risks, and impermissibly alter the status quo they have unilaterally created,” they said. “The Court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed.” Jones and Schwalb added that they believe the administration is violating the Commemorative Works Act by bypassing specific congressional authorization and violating the Height of Buildings Act by constructing an arch that’s set to exceed 130 feet in height. They also alleged violations of the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act. Jones, in a statement Saturday, said, “Virginia takes immense pride in being home to Arlington National Cemetery, the final resting place of generations of American heroes who gave their lives defending our nation. President Trump’s illegal vanity project is an affront to this hallowed ground and the extraordinary sacrifices it represents. The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place. We will vigorously litigate to protect its sanctity and honor the legacy of those who made the ultimate sacrifice.” Schwalb said, “Construction of the Arch is flagrantly illegal and will cause serious, immediate, and irreparable harm to the District and its residents. We’re filing this lawsuit now to protect DC’s unique interests and critical role in preserving the safeguards that keep our nation’s capital beautiful and safe,” in a separate statement. Earlier this year, the National Capital Planning Commission, led by Trump appointees, approved initial plans for construction of the arch, one of President Donald Trump’s efforts to remake Washington in his own image during this term. The commission is set to vote on final plans for the arch on Nov. 5. In a statement, White House spokesperson David Ingle told NBC News on Saturday, “The Triumphal Arch in Memorial Circle is going to be one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world. It will serve as a gateway to Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike, serving as a visual reminder of the noble sacrifices borne by so many American heroes throughout our 250 year history so we can enjoy our freedoms today. President Trump will continue to honor our veterans and give the greatest Nation on earth — America — the glory it deserves.” Ingle did not address a direct question from NBC News about the lawsuit filed Saturday. Renderings obtained by NBC News in April show that the arch is slated to feature winged eagles, Lady Liberty and a line from the Pledge of Allegiance. In September, the president said on Truth Social that the arch would also serve a national security function because it will be outfitted to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.” But final plans and renderings submitted to the NCPC do not include the military upgrades the president wrote about. Trump has used national security as an argument in favor of other construction projects that have faced legal battles, like the new ballroom he is building at the White House. In addition to functioning as a gathering space for large events at the White House, the president has said, the addition will also house a military complex to be built underneath the ballroom. “When completed in the Summer of 2028, the magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex will be something that the entire Country is very proud of,” the president wrote in an August Truth Social post after the Supreme Court allowed construction of the ballroom to continue, rebuffing a legal challenge from the National Trust for Historic Preservation. The president has also drawn the ire of locals with a proposed plan to renovate the East Potomac Golf Links course in Washington, despite legal hurdles with that project. In a post on Truth Social Thursday, Trump said why he favored renovating the golf course. “East Potomac Golf Course is highly dangerous, dilapidated, and absolutely disgusting. Below are new photos of the deplorable conditions of the driving range building, including excrement in the stairwell. The gaping holes in the driving range’s ‘protective’ netting are highly hazardous. Golf balls soar through the holes at high speed and hit unexpecting Golfers — including a White House staffer who was, sadly, hit violently in the chest,” the president wrote. He has promised to turn the course into “a World Class Championship Golf Course.”

articles.title: Who are Ilhan Omar’s lawyers? Meet the high-powered Dem attorneys the embattled rep hired
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar has hired Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, attorneys who represented Biden, House Democrats in Trump impeachment, and E. Jean Carroll.
articles.body: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has tapped two high-powered Washington, D.C.-based attorneys who have previously represented elected officials at the highest echelon of American politics. Amid dueling federal investigations — one for immigration fraud and another for financial disclosure discrepancies — the embattled Somali-born lawmaker hired Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, according to a CBS report, both of whom are partners at Hecker Fink LLP. The attorneys have in the past represented Democrat clients and taken on left-leaning cases — especially those taking aim at President Donald Trump, his administration and his supporters. ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS Amy Jeffress Jeffress is a former federal prosecutor whose biography says she tried more than 40 cases during a decade in the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the District of Columbia, where she was Chief of the National Security Section. She has also been a Department of Justice (DOJ) Attaché. She served as former President Joe Biden's attorney in his lawsuit against the DOJ earlier this year. In that case, Biden sought to halt the release of audio recordings between himself and his "Promise Me, Dad" book ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer. The audio was recorded in 2016 and 2017, and were subject to a FOIA request from the Heritage Foundation in 2024. They were cited during special counsel Robert Hur's investigation into whether Biden illegally retained classified information from his term as vice president, and piqued the interest of conservatives demanding answers about Biden's mental acuity. The court declined to block the release of the recordings where Biden ad frequent memory lapses, and they were made public in July. FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE Before her time at Hecker Fink, Jeffress, a Yale Law graduate from 1992, served as counsel for then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and the Democrat-led House January 6 committee, which spent two years investigating the riot at the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. She represented the committee when it was sued by a Trump campaign spokesperson, Taylor Budowich, after the committee subpoenaed his bank records. Jeffress also represented Trump foe and former FBI attorney Lisa Page — a key figure in the left's Russiagate conspiracy theory — during congressional scrutiny into the FBI's handling of the matter. Page later sued the DOJ for releasing her text messages with her then-FBI colleague and lover Peter Strzok. In the messages, Strzok assuaged Page's concerns that Trump would become president by vowing that the FBI would stop it, and referred to an "insurance policy" against his presidency. That case was settled in 2024. ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME Jeffress is married to U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of Washington, D.C., who in May ruled that it was illegal for the the John F. Kennedy Performing Arts Center to add Trump's name. Trump publicly criticized Cooper as "highly conflicted," due to his relationship with Jeffress. Joshua Matz Matz is also a partner at Hecker Fink. He graduated from Harvard Law, and clerked for former Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy. "Joshua’s practice has long included a focus on democracy and elections," his biography page says. He represented the state of Pennsylvania in defending the certification of its election results, including arguing before the Supreme Court. ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION He was counsel to House Democrats during both failed impeachment attempts against Trump during his first term in office. Matz also represented E. Jean Carroll in two separate civil cases against Trump related to his denial of her of sexual assault claims against him. He was never criminally charged. In 2022, Carroll accused Trump of defaming her in his denial of her account of an incident she claims happened in 1996. A New York jury found Trump liable for defamation and for sexual assault. Prior to that case, in 2019, a jury awarded Carroll $83.3 million for defamation stemming from other comments made by Trump. Matz represented students, parents and teachers who opposed Florida's Parental Rights in Education Act, which his biography describes as the "Don't Say Gay" law, which restricted teaching students about sexual orientation and gender identity. He also successfully represented Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear when he was sued for COVID-19 lockdowns, including school closures, and victims of the 2017 "Unite the Right" rally in Charlottesville. In a video message posted to her social media earlier this month, the lawmaker pleaded with her supporters to keep sending money, noting that her fight against the investigations would be costly. articles.title: A cure for Trump? Why Democratic doctors are running in the 2026 midterms
articles.summary: Democratic doctors aim to convert the backlash against the Trump administration’s health policies into midterm votes.
articles.body:
San Francisco, California – Three words stretch across the front page of Richard Pan’s campaign website: “Public Health Hero”.

The California paediatrician is part of a wave of public health professionals angling for a seat in the United States Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections.

The American College of Gastroenterology has estimated that as many as 25 physicians could win congressional office this election cycle, a record number that would usher in "a new generation of physician-lawmakers".

But while many of the incumbents are Republicans, experts say there has been a notable rise in the number of Democratic doctors and healthcare workers on the ballot.

Some are competing in the highest-profile races of the year. Abdul El-Sayed, a physician and former public health official, is locked in a close race for Michigan's open Senate seat.

In South Carolina, meanwhile, paediatrician Annie Andrews has turned what would normally be a safe Senate seat for Republicans into a battleground.

Experts and advocacy groups credit the growing number of Democratic doctors-turned-politicians, in part, to frustration with Republican President Donald Trump.

Democrats, they say, are tapping into public rage not only over rising healthcare costs but also Trump-era policies they see as anti-scientific.

“Scientists themselves have woken up. We cannot just abandon the public forum to all of this misinformation, disinformation,” said Eric Feigl-Ding, an epidemiologist who founded Vax PAC, a political advocacy group that backs candidates who support responsible vaccine policies.

Feigl-Ding sees the surge in political participation not as an act of partisanship but rather as a chance to advocate for responsible healthcare policies.

“It's not like public health is rolling up our sleeves and getting dirty in the pigsty,” Feigl-Ding said. “What public health is doing is immunising ourselves against politics.”

articles.title: El-Sayed drops Stevens from campaign event
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) told Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), his once primary opponent, to stay away from his campaign events and disinvited her from a planned appearance on Sunday, a source familiar confirmed to NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcasting partner. The source said El-Sayed does not want the ongoing fight with Stevens to distract…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) told Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), his once primary opponent, to stay away from his campaign events and disinvited her from a planned appearance on Sunday, a source familiar confirmed to NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcasting partner.

The source said El-Sayed does not want the ongoing fight with Stevens to distract from the issues in the final days of his hard-fought Senate campaign.

A spokesperson for Stevens did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

El-Sayed was set to appear alongside Stevens and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.) at a church in Detroit, a show of unity despite some harsh words exchanged between the two candidates throughout the week.

Stevens released a statement saying she had accepted Clyburn’s invitation to appear alongside El-Sayed, but still criticized the Senate nominee for not condemning an ad that appeared to blame Israel for high grocery prices.

“The ad did not invent its argument; it dramatized one Dr. El-Sayed has made in his own words throughout this campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, healthcare, and child care,” Stevens said in her statement. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well.”

The ad was run digitally and was bought by an outside progressive group, not El-Sayed’s campaign.

El-Sayed shot back in a statement on Friday, saying Stevens is focused on rehashing their August primary, which he narrowly won.

“So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics,” El-Sayed said in a statement posted to the social platform X.

Support for Israel was a major issue in the Democratic primary. Stevens was backed by millions in funds from pro-Israel lobbying groups, which El-Sayed criticized her for. The Democratic Senate nominee is critical of Israel and has called for the U.S. to stop sending aid to the country.

Since the primary, courting Jewish voters has been a hurdle for El-Sayed. His Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has worked to earn the support of disaffected Democrats, including those who are Jewish.

While Stevens told CNN this week that she still plans to vote for El-Sayed, her fiancé, who is Jewish, announced that he would be voting for Rogers.

articles.title: Michigan man charged with allegedly threatening to kill Kash Patel, ‘his associate’
articles.summary: A Michigan man was charged Friday with allegedly threatening the life of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel and “his associate.” The U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Eastern District of Michigan said in a news release that 42-year-old Anthony Daniel Palazzolo was arrested and appeared in federal court on Friday after he sent…
articles.body:
A Michigan man was charged Friday with allegedly threatening the life of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel and “his associate.”

The U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Eastern District of Michigan said in a news release that 42-year-old Anthony Daniel Palazzolo was arrested and appeared in federal court on Friday after he sent a threatening Facebook message earlier this month to an associate of Patel.

In the Oct. 8 message, Palazzolo allegedly wrote to the associate, who was not named, that he had “put out a hit” against him.

A detention hearing has been set for Nov. 2.

Reports of threats against government officials and elected leaders have been on the rise in recent years. A CBS News investigation published in February found there were 126 people charged last year for making threats to federal and top state officials.

Ahead of the midterm elections, many lawmakers reported suspicious packages containing white powder had been delivered to their home district and state offices.

Additionally, law enforcement arrested two men earlier this month who separately made death threats against Reps. Keith Self (R-Texas) and Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.).

In a social media post following this threat, Self thanked the FBI and local law enforcement for their response.

“My family and I are safe, and I remain focused on serving the people of Texas’ 3rd District,” Self wrote. “Preserving our constitutional republic from radical Islam means accepting the costs that come with it—name-calling, threats, and worse.”

Moskowitz similarly thanked law enforcement partners and said he and his family were safe following the incident.
