articles.title: Why are so many young Americans dying?
articles.summary: Recent research indicates a significant rise in mortality among Americans aged 25 to 44 between 2010 and 2021, driven by a combination of substance abuse, chronic diseases, and social factors.
articles.body:
We’re constantly told that America is the greatest country on Earth, hands down. Questioning that narrative invites eye-rolls and plenty of criticism. But question it, we must.

If America is so great, why are so many young people dying?

Between 2010 and 2021, as recent research from Virginia Commonwealth University shows, mortality among Americans ages 25 to 44 rose by 71.2 percent. People are meeting their maker during the very years they should be meeting a potential spouse.

The classic American playbook is incredibly simple, at least in theory. It encourages young adults to get an education, climb the career ladder, settle down, raise a family, and do their best not to get divorced .

Mortality data suggest the script falls apart just as people try to follow it. America excels at adding extra months onto the end of an 80-year-old life with extraordinarily expensive ICU stays. At the very same time, it routinely fails to keep a 32-year-old alive long enough to see their kids enter middle school.

The human damage extends far beyond the coroner’s office. A single premature death tears a family apart. Children grow up with empty seats at the dinner table. Parents bury adult children who were supposed to be choosing their senior care facilities. Men and women become widows before their first gray hairs appear. Communities lose plumbers, teachers, police officers, and neighbors who should have kept the local economy running for another 30 years.

Public discussions often default to the fentanyl crisis when the issue of young mortality arises. Illicit synthetic opioids certainly kill too many people, but drug overdoses tell only part of the story. Young Americans are dying from a bizarre cocktail of self-inflicted and biological disasters. Suicide rates remain high. Alcohol-related liver disease, fatal traffic wrecks, homicides, high blood pressure, and metabolic disorders are all claiming people in their 20s and 30s.

Diseases once reserved for world-weary retirees are making a triumphant comeback in people who still remember their high school gym class locker codes. Hypertension and fatty liver disease are moving down the demographic chart at an alarming rate. Young bodies are showing the structural wear and tear of 60-year-olds.

Modern political commentary loves to blame systemic failure for every national ailment. Institutional problems clearly exist, yet much of this crisis comes down to personal habits. Medical science can treat a gunshot wound and clear a blocked artery, but it can’t force a person to stop drinking a gallon of vodka a week. Technology cannot step in when someone decides to drive 90 miles an hour while sending memes on an icy interstate. Ultra-processed junk food, sedentary screen time, heavy drinking, and untreated mental illnesses represent personal choices that no government agency can micromanage away.

The U.S. spends trillions of dollars annually on healthcare , far more than any other wealthy nation. Yet the return on that astronomical investment is a declining life expectancy. European nations spend a fraction of what Americans shell out, yet their citizens routinely survive into their 80s and 90s without relying on advanced biological therapies. High-tech medical interventions are lousy substitutes for daily self-care and a respectable lifestyle.

Geography compounds the risk in ways that look almost arbitrary. A child born in one zip code can expect to live a decade longer than a child born 50 miles away. Local economics, regional food cultures, smoking habits, and access to trauma care create significant survival disparities across state lines. The differences reflect sobering realities about local employment, education and everyday habits.

Social isolation makes matters worse. High-speed internet access and infinite streaming content have arrived alongside a massive drop in face-to-face human connection. Young adults have thousands of online followers but no one to pick them up from the hospital after a minor procedure. Chronic loneliness raises stress hormones and disrupts sleep . It accelerates inflammation and pushes people toward destructive vices like alcohol, hard drugs and self-harm.

Traditional public health frameworks analyze each cause of death as an isolated event. One department handles addiction, another tracks heart disease, and a third studies traffic safety. That bureaucratic division misses the larger pattern. When multiple completely different causes of death spike simultaneously within the exact same age group, the culture itself is creating something that physicians and strongly worded policies can’t fix.

A genuinely healthy society ought to measure its basic success by whether an average citizen has the opportunity to age gracefully into grandparenthood. America is failing that test miserably, one premature obituary at a time.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

articles.title: Major US children's hospital opens historic detransition clinic after $10M legal showdown

articles.body: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced Tuesday that the nation’s first-ever detransition clinic has opened at Texas Children’s Hospital following a $10 million settlement with the state. The announcement comes after Paxton reached a settlement with TCH in May, finalized in August, requiring the hospital to pay $10 million to resolve government claims and separately establish and fund a detransition clinic. The new clinic provides "detransition-related medical care to patients through age 21, along with detransition-related obstetric and gynecologic care to patients older than 21," according to Paxton's office. "In accordance with my settlement with Texas Children’s Hospital, the nation’s first-ever Detransition Clinic is now open," Paxton said in a statement. A LANDMARK TEXAS RULING BREATHES NEW LIFE INTO ONE DETRANSITIONER'S QUEST FOR JUSTICE "Together, we will protect our children and defeat the dangerous ideology that has inflicted irreversible harm on innocent kids," he continued. Tuesday's announcement comes as Paxton is running for election in Texas' 2026 Senate race. President Donald Trump campaigned in two separate Texas cities, Corpus Christi and Lubbock, on Tuesday in an effort to boost Paxton's Senate bid. The Trump administration has been targeting initiatives related to transgender people in recent months. Trump announced in August that his administration will cease providing funding for gender transition surgeries using Medicaid for minors. Paxton's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. A TCH spokesperson told Fox News Digital on Wednesday that the hospital prioritizes providing patients "the highest standard of care," including through the detransition clinic. "First and foremost, patients and families are at the center of all we do and we will always provide the highest standard of care, including through this clinic, which formalizes the supportive, multidisciplinary services we have and will continue to deliver," the TCH spokesperson said. "All services provided will be within our hospital’s existing licensure and scope," the spokesperson added. The clinic is operational and we are complying with all requirements in the settlement agreement." The TCH spokesperson also told Fox News Digital that the hospital is "actively triaging prospective patients" for the detransition clinic. "Protecting the privacy of our patients and their families is a top priority, thus we are unable to share patient information," the spokesperson stated. articles.title: D.C. and Virginia sue to block Trump’s proposed triumphal arch
articles.summary: The D.C. government and the commonwealth of Virginia sued Saturday to block construction of President Donald Trump’s planned triumphal arch, calling it a “fl...
articles.body:
The D.C. government and the commonwealth of Virginia sued Saturday to block construction of President Donald Trump's planned triumphal arch, calling it a "flagrantly unlawful" project that will forever change the landscape of the nation's capital.

The lawsuit is the latest attempt to stop the 250-foot-tall arch, which Trump hopes to build near Arlington National Cemetery and says will commemorate the nation's 250th birthday. The administration would like to begin construction as soon as next week.

The two jurisdictions are asking U.S. District Judge Tanya S. Chutkan to halt the plan and argue that they have "indisputable standing" to bring their lawsuit because the towering arch would have tangible, negative effects on the region - an argument that distinguishes their lawsuit from others that have tried to stop Trump's construction projects.

D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb (D) said the arch construction would cause "serious, immediate and irreparable harm to the District and its residents," while Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones (D) said "Trump's illegal vanity project" would be an affront to Arlington National Cemetery and the "extraordinary sacrifices it represents."

"The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place," Jones said in a statement. "We will vigorously litigate to protect its sanctity and honor the legacy of those who made the ultimate sacrifice."

The arch already faces legal peril. In a separate case brought by three Vietnam War veterans and a historic preservationist, Chutkan on Friday signaled she might block it.

Asked about the lawsuit, a White House spokesman reiterated the administration's position that the arch would be "one of the most iconic landmarks" in the world.

Spokespeople for the Interior Department, which is managing the project, did not immediately respond to questions about the new lawsuit.

The administration has acknowledged that the arch will unavoidably harm local historic sites by altering views, and that it will divert traffic and create loud noise during years of planned construction, among other disruptions. Officials have said that those harms are not significant enough to halt what the administration has deemed a "high-priority project."

The Trump administration has also tried to defend the arch and the president's other construction projects by claiming that litigants lack standing - the legal grounds to sue - because they cannot show that they would be directly harmed. That argument swayed the Supreme Court this summer in a case about Trump's White House ballroom. The justices ruled 5-4 that a historic preservationist likely could not prove that she would be harmed by the project - and cleared the way for Trump to keep building.

D.C. and Virginia say harms to the region would be irreversible if Trump's project proceeds. In their court filing, the jurisdictions argue that the arch would harm the region's security and emergency preparedness, disrupt traffic, degrade the environment and run afoul of the Height Act, which caps building heights at 130 feet in D.C. - a defining feature of the city's architecture intended to preserve views of the Washington Monument and the U.S. Capitol. The arch would be nearly double that height.

They also say the arch is illegal because Congress has not authorized it, and because the National Park Service failed to follow laws requiring "appropriate consultation before undertaking a project that would transform the District's physical landscape and upend its historic plan."

The Trump administration has said construction could begin by Thursday if the National Capital Planning Commission - a federal review panel that oversees major projects in the region - approves the arch proposal at its meeting that day.

Trump has packed the commission with allies, and its chairman has already said he plans to vote for the project. The Interior Department could then quickly green-light construction, officials have said.

Lawyers for D.C. and Virginia argue that if the court fails to act now, the administration could swiftly shift to a new argument - as officials did last year with Trump's ballroom - that once construction on project begins, it will be too late to stop.

"The court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed," they wrote in the filing.

D.C. Council Chairman Phil Mendelson (D), who has served on the National Capital Planning Commission since 2012, wrote in a declaration to the court that the speed of the commission's review has been "unprecedented" and insufficient. The commission advanced the proposed arch through key reviews within five weeks, compared with the years-long process to evaluate typical projects, he said.

"Congress established a process for approving memorials in Washington for good reason. What we commemorate, where we commemorate it, and how a memorial fits into Washington's historic landscape are important decisions that deserve careful consideration," Mendelson said in an accompanying statement. "The proposed Arch has not gone through that process."

Trump has said he hopes to build the arch on Memorial Circle, a traffic roundabout near the south end of Arlington Memorial Bridge and tucked inside Washington's boundaries. Administration officials have laid out a plan to work 20 hours per day, year-round, for several years to construct the arch.

The speed and scope of the president's project - a planned five-level "concrete structure clad in granite," as federal officials have described it - have alarmed historic preservationists, architects, parks advocates and local groups that say its effects on the region would be irrevocable.

The arch would permanently disrupt historic architectural designs by competing with the Washington Monument, local officials argue. It would also obstruct the sight line between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, a memorial to Robert E. Lee. The historic preservation officers from both jurisdictions have raised concerns about a lack of review required by law.

But the arch would also cause other logistical headaches, D.C. and Virginia officials say, such as year-round construction for two to three years that would temporarily and permanently change traffic patterns on a busy artery - with potentially serious implications.

They note the arch construction could hamper emergency vehicles at the foot of a bridge that is a designated evacuation route.

"The construction-related closures of the Circle, new pedestrian crossings, and additional pedestrian and vehicular traffic after construction is finished will all complicate evacuations from and emergency response in the District," they write.

And in a highly restricted airspace, the towering height of the proposed arch would "pose risks to air safety," which will require local officials to spend significant resources adjusting emergency preparedness plans, D.C. and Virginia officials say.

D.C. leaders have not previously sued to block Trump's construction projects, including the ballroom, the changes to the East Potomac golf course and other projects that have drawn complaints.

In a hearing Friday in the separate lawsuit seeking to block the arch, Chutkan independently raised questions about how the arch would affect traffic patterns and other potential disruptions to the region. An administration lawyer told the judge that he was not prepared to talk about traffic patterns because that issue was not germane to that case.

Chutkan questioned what harm would be caused by waiting several months versus beginning construction as soon as next week.

"What is the rush to put this arch up?" she asked.
